To study the magnitude and direction of surface tension, the textbook uses a rectangular metal frame with a movable side of length $l$, labeled $AB$, that can move in a vertical plane with little friction (Figure 69).
Once a soap film forms in the frame, wire $AB$ tends to move as the film tends to reduce its surface area.
The film's force on wire $AB$ lies in the film's plane and is perpendicular to the wire.

A resultant force $\vec F_1$ opposing the film's pull keeps the wire in equilibrium, allowing surface tension to be studied through the balance of forces.
To provide $\vec F_1$, the textbook attaches a soft spring fixed to a stand to the wire (Figure 69).
Here, $\vec F_1$ is the combined force of the spring and the wire's weight, not necessarily the spring force alone.

When wire $AB$ is in equilibrium, the textbook's vector convention gives:
$\vec F_1=-2\vec F$.

The minus sign indicates opposite directions, and the factor comes from the film's two surfaces.
It does not mean that the tension of a single interface automatically doubles.
repairs.after:
A force is a push or a pull.
The size of a force is called its magnitude.
We can study the size and direction of surface tension with a soap film.
The textbook uses an upright rectangular metal frame.
One side is a straight wire of length $l$, labeled $AB$ (Figure 69).
The wire slides up and down in a vertical plane.
This is the upright flat area of the frame.
There is little friction, the rubbing that resists sliding.
Dipping the frame into soapy water leaves a thin layer of soapy liquid across it.
This layer is the soap film.
Surface area means the amount of space a surface covers.
Once the film forms, wire $AB$ tends to move as the film tends to make its surface smaller.
The film pulls on wire $AB$ along the flat surface of the film.
The pull is perpendicular to the wire.
Perpendicular means at a right angle.

A second pull balances the film's pull.
The resultant force $\vec F_1$ is the combined force of the spring and the wire's weight.
Resultant here means the result of combining those two forces only.
The film's pull is the separate force that this resultant balances.
To provide $\vec F_1$, the textbook attaches a soft spring to the wire.
The spring's other end is fixed to a stand (Figure 69).
In this setup, $\vec F_1$ points down, and the film pulls up.

The letter F names the pull from one surface of the film.
An interface is a surface where the film meets its surroundings.
The thin film has two interfaces, one on each side.
When conditions at both interfaces are the same, each surface gives an equally strong upward pull.
Their pulls add in this setup.
The arrow over a force letter shows that the force has a direction.
A force described by its size and direction is called a vector.
When wire $AB$ stays still because the forces balance, it is in equilibrium.
The pulls are still present.
The combined downward pull and the total upward pull are equal in size.
The textbook writes this balance as follows:
$\vec F_1=-2\vec F$.

The minus sign shows that the forces point in opposite directions.
The factor comes from the film's two surfaces.
A single interface supplies its own pull.
Doubling applies here because two equal interface pulls point in the same direction.

repairs.before:
Here, $\vec F$ is the force exerted on the wire by one of the film's two surfaces (Figure 70).
When conditions at the two interfaces, where the film meets its surroundings, are the same, their forces have equal magnitudes and point in the same direction in the illustrated geometry, so they add.
The two-interface factor for this soap film cannot be applied unconditionally to a single interface.
repairs.after:
Here, $\vec F$ is the pull from one of the film's two surfaces (Figure 70).
This diagram looks at the same wire AB end-on.
End-on means looking along the wire from one end.
The wire appears as a circle in this view.
The two sides shown belong to one thin film.
Each surface pulls the wire upward.
Each interface is where the liquid film meets its surroundings.
When conditions at both interfaces are the same, the two pulls are equally strong.
They point the same way in this setup, so they add.
A single interface supplies only its own pull.
The doubling rule needs two equal interface pulls in the same direction.

When the wire moves downward through a distance $h$, suppose the motion is approximately quasistatic: slow enough to remain close to equilibrium.
The magnitude of the balancing external resultant is $F_1=2F$, and its work is:

$A=F_1h=2Fh.$
(5-2)

This work is done by the combined spring force and weight.
The gravitational work for the same displacement must not be added again.

During downward extension, the external resultant and displacement point in the same direction, so this work is positive;
the film's opposing pull does negative work.

The work expression also assumes negligible friction and viscous losses, meaning energy dissipated by the liquid's resistance to flow.
Interface conditions must remain stable and the force approximately constant.

Now let the wire move down.
In the first diagram, the lower dashed line marks the same wire in its later position.
The labels A' and B' mark its ends there.
These labels are read as A prime and B prime.
A prime mark identifies the later position of the same end.
The downward travel distance is $h$.
Use the actual travel in the experiment for this distance.
Suppose the wire moves slowly enough for the forces to stay nearly balanced.
This is called approximately quasistatic motion.
The wire stays close to equilibrium during the motion.
Friction and viscous losses are negligible in this model.
Negligible means small enough to leave out.
Viscous losses are energy wasted by the liquid's resistance to flow.
Conditions at both interfaces stay stable, and the force stays approximately constant.
Constant means staying the same during the motion.
The size of the combined downward force is $F_1=2F$.
Work is energy transferred by a force as an object moves through a distance.
The letter A names the amount of work done by this combined force.
The next equation multiplies the force by the downward travel distance.

$A=F_1h=2Fh.$
(5-2)

This work comes from both the spring force and the wire's weight.
The weight is already included in the combined force.
Counting gravity's work again would count the same contribution twice.

During downward extension, the combined force and the movement both point down.
The work done by this force is positive.
The film pulls up, opposite to the movement.
The work done by the film's pull is negative.

In this model, the external work increases the film's surface-energy contribution.
The textbook calls this "surface energy".
More precisely, for a reversible process at constant temperature, the surface work corresponds to an increase in surface free energy, the energy measure relevant to reversible work under these conditions.

It should not be equated unconditionally with the change in the whole system's internal energy.
Initially, the area of one surface is $S_1$, and the textbook writes the film's surface energy as $U_{\text{surface}1}=2\sigma S_1$ because the film has two surfaces of equal area.
It writes the final surface energy as $U_{\text{surface}2}=2\sigma S_2$.

These expressions assume an approximately constant surface tension coefficient, with temperature and composition stable and the surrounding medium unchanged.
Thus:
repairs.after:
Making more film surface requires energy in this model.
The external work supplies energy for the extra surface.
We consider an ideal slow change called a reversible change.
Reversible means the change can be undone without energy being wasted by friction or resistance to flow.
The temperature stays the same.
This is called constant temperature.
Under these conditions, the surface work increases the film's surface free energy.
In this model, surface free energy measures the energy needed to make the surface at that temperature.
The textbook calls its surface-energy contribution "surface energy".

The whole system's internal energy includes all the energy stored inside it.
A process at fixed temperature can still exchange heat with its surroundings.
The surface-work increase alone does not tell us the whole system's internal-energy change.

Area means how much space a surface covers.
S one names the area of one surface before the wire moves.
S two names the area of that same surface after it moves.
U surface one and U surface two name the model's surface-energy amounts before and after this change.
The contact length is the length of wire touched by one surface.
The surface tension coefficient, called sigma, gives the pull from one surface per unit of contact length.
Per unit length means for each equal unit of wire length.
Sigma also gives the surface free energy per unit of surface area in this model.
These formulas use an approximately constant surface tension coefficient.
The temperature and the liquid's composition stay stable.
Composition means what the liquid is made of.
The surrounding medium also stays the same.
The medium is the material around the film.

Initially, one surface has area $S_1$.
The film has two surfaces of equal area.
Its initial surface energy is $U_{\text{surface}1}=2\sigma S_1$.
Its final surface energy is $U_{\text{surface}2}=2\sigma S_2$.

The next equation subtracts the initial amount from the final amount to find the increase.

We can now simplify the equation.
A factor is a quantity multiplied by another quantity.
Both sides contain the factor two times h.
The downward travel is greater than zero, so this common factor is not zero.
Dividing each side by the same nonzero factor removes it from both sides.
This step is called cancellation.
It leaves a rule connecting the pull from one surface to the contact length.

The boundary is the edge where the film meets the wire.
Here, the interface is uniform and flat.
Uniform means it has the same properties along the contact.
A longer straight contact gives a larger pull under the same conditions.

repairs.before:
Surface tension acts tangentially to the liquid surface and perpendicular to the chosen surface boundary.
In Figures 69 and 70, this means within the film's plane and perpendicular to wire $AB$.
For a curved surface, use the local tangent plane and the boundary's direction at each point.

Forces along different boundary segments cannot simply be added without considering their directions.
The boundary length here is the length of contact between one surface and the movable wire, not the entire frame's perimeter.
Under the same interface conditions, the force magnitude is proportional to this boundary length, with surface tension coefficient $\sigma$ as the proportionality constant.

The force-to-boundary-length relation in formula (5-4) gives units of newtons per meter.
These are equivalent to joules per square meter from the surface-energy viewpoint, since J/m$^2=$N m/m$^2$ $=$N/m.
repairs.after:
The pictured wire is straight.
In Figures 69 and 70, the pull runs along the film and perpendicular to wire $AB$.
Perpendicular means at a right angle.
The boundary is the edge where the film meets the wire.
A tangential pull runs along a surface.
Surface tension gives this pull at a right angle to the boundary.
For a curved surface, imagine a tiny patch at the edge.
Its local tangent plane is an imaginary flat plane touching the patch at that point.
This plane shows the patch's flat direction there.
The pull lies in this plane and at a right angle to the boundary's direction at that point.
Apply this rule at each point along the edge.

A boundary segment is one part of the edge.
Forces on different boundary segments may point in different directions.
Their directions must be considered when adding these forces.
Simply adding their sizes can give the wrong total.
Here, the boundary length is the contact length between one surface and the movable wire.
Use this contact length, rather than the whole frame's perimeter.
Perimeter means the total length around the frame.
Under the same interface conditions, the pull is proportional to this contact length.
Proportional means that the pull and length increase by the same factor.
The proportionality constant gives the pull per unit of contact length.
Here, that constant is the surface tension coefficient $\sigma$.

A newton is a unit of force.
A joule is a unit of energy.
The force itself is measured in newtons.
In formula (5-4), sigma has units of newtons per meter.
The letter N stands for newtons, and m stands for meters.
A square meter is a unit of area.
The letter J stands for joules.
From the surface-energy viewpoint, sigma also has units of joules per square meter.
The units for sigma agree because J/m$^2=$N m/m$^2$ $=$N/m.
